title: 🚗 Lucid has too many cars 🚙
body_text: Liberty Mutual, an insurance company, recently debuted a new mascot: a yellow puffball named Liberty Biberty . It joins the ranks of America’s surprising deep bench insurance mascots: the Gecko from Geico , Flo from Progressive , and of course its LiMu Emu and Doug, also from Liberty Mutual. It’s unclear why an industry built around deductibles and actuarial tables has produced some of advertising’s most elaborate fictional universes, Jeff Maurer writes . At this rate, we’re one Super Bowl commercial away from learning the Geico Gecko’s origin story. As fuel prices reach record highs, Americans have another reason to switch from their gas-guzzlers to an electric vehicle or hybrid. So far, that hasn’t come to rescue Lucid Motors . The American EV company delivered 3,806 vehicles in the quarter ending September 30, coming in well below the roughly 4,700 analysts were expecting. It also produced only 2,954 cars in the quarter, coming in below Wall Street estimates and down 38% from the previous quarter. For the past year Lucid has produced more cars than it has sold.The company said it is now reducing stockpile amid a cost-cutting campaign. “As part of its operating reset, Lucid continued to align production with near-term demand,” it said. As is often the case, this appears to be a Lucid-specific issue rather than an industry bellwether. All other signs seem to suggest that after poo-pooing EVs for several years, US consumers are starting to look at cars that may hurt their wallet less. Both Tesla and Rivian , two of the largest electric vehicle makers in the world, reported more deliveries than expected during the same quarter. Toyota recently reported that its “electrified vehicle,” consisting mostly of hybrids, kept it afloat in its most recent quarterly report . General Motors plans to introduce hybrid models into its US lineup, a company executive told CNBC on Monday , telling the outlet “we’re not tone-deaf to our customers.” Lucid Motors has failed to make a dent in the electric vehicle market for several reasons. The company’s new CEO, Silvio Napoli, started in June and immediately cut staff and eliminated a second production shift at its Arizona factory in an effort to “simplify the company.” Now he’s trying to shrink the pile of unsold cars, too. title: 🍂 Prime before the fall
body_text: The announcements for the winners of this year’s Nobel Prize awards got underway yesterday, as US psychiatrist Karl Deisseroth and two German colleagues received this year’s prize in Physiology or Medicine for their research on the inner workings of the human brain. The three scientists, who will share the ~$1.2 million prize money, can only hope that their work stands the test of time a little longer than the recipient of the same award 100 years ago. Danish pathologist Johannes Fibiger picked up the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine in 1926 for his work identifying a parasitic worm as a cause of stomach cancer in rats, but his research was proved wrong only a few years later , and the award has gone down as one of the rare cases of a mistakenly awarded Nobel Prize. Seemingly unperturbed by the fact that no one has ever referred to its latter-year promotional period by its official (and overlong) title, Amazon is pushing its “Prime Big Deal Days” again, with ads and somehow-not-sponsored editorials for various offers inevitably cluttering news feeds and inboxes today and tomorrow. This two-day discount window is the younger and smaller sibling of Amazon’s original summertime Prime Day, having first been introduced four years ago and lasting for just 48 hours, compared to the four-day stretch of the June 2026 event. The promotions are big business for Amazon, as investors who keep a keen eye on the company’s quarterly reports will be aware, after it shifted the summer event to see the sales uptick in Q2 rather than Q3 this year . Luckily for Amazon, it seems that the secondary event is gathering a little more steam this year in comparison to previous editions. While summer searches for the main event have dwindled a little in the years since their peak eight years ago, US interest in the October Prime Day has reached a new high this year, according to partially complete data from Google . Despite ongoing questions around whether Amazon’s promotional events actually offer customers value for money, the figures suggest that shoppers are still eager to find out for themselves. Even as parts of Amazon’s business that aren’t selling-you-things-online-for-cheap — such as its burgeoning AI and custom chip businesses — continue to grow , online retail sales still account for the lion’s share of its top-line revenue figures, making shifting products at lower prices around Prime Days a bit of a no-brainer for the company. Bezos’ company also has more paying users to target with discounts and deals than ever before. When the company hosted its first Prime Day in July 2015 to celebrate its 20th anniversary, just 54 million US shoppers used Prime; last year, that figure had ballooned to a staggering 201 million. That’s how much “Digger,” the Tom Cruise-led satire that marks Warner Bros’ last release before its $111 billion merger with Paramount is expected to close today, made across North American theaters in its opening weekend. The disappointing haul (down, even, from the $12 million to $15 million that Warner execs had pessimistically penciled in) is Cruise’s lowest domestic debut since “Lions for Lambs” in 2007, per The Hollywood Reporter . With a reported budget of around $160 million, the underwhelming first weekend box office figure could set “Digger” up as one of the biggest commercial flops in recent history. In sad news for Cruise heads around the world, it’s also looking like yet another setback on the megastar’s decades-long quest to get his hands on a competitive Oscar, with his latest departure from the action roles he’s become known for currently sitting at a lowly 51% critics’ rating on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes . Chips and dip: Intel dropped yesterday after Elon Musk confirmed talks between TSMC and his Terafab chip venture around potential collaboration. EV sales in the EU hit a new record for January to August this year, according to a study from a Brussels environmental advocacy agency, with new research showing that deliveries may rose 45% from 2025 to 1.64 million. OpenAI announced that it will test new visual ad format to ChatGPT, which it noted reaches 1.2 billion people per week, debuting the new style with people generating images on the platform. Meta and Microsoft are working to get their own employees to use Anthropic’s Claude less, The Information reports . The US currently reigns supreme, counting 432 prizes, compared to the UK which sits in a distant second place with a tally of 148, per World Population Review . title: 👟 Nike’s plan to make Jordans cool again
body_text: One lawyer learned the hard way that ChatGPT is not a witness. New Mexico attorney Stephen Aarons used ChatGPT to help write a brief for a murder appeal — only for it to invent witnesses and testimony that never existed. “It’s little comfort to know that my stupidity is what brings us together this afternoon,” Aarons told five judges . The court fined him $5,000 and kicked him off the case. Stocks finished up on Friday, pushing the week into positive territory. It’s been a rough few years for Nike , and so far its comeback plans haven’t managed to get sales growing again. Its next act: rethinking Jordan. The brand accounted for 13% of Nike’s global business last quarter, but revenue fell by the mid-teens. On a call with analysts on Thursday, CEO Elliott Hill offered a pretty straightforward diagnosis: “Simply put, we've been oversupplying our iconic retro product, asking them to do too much.” The company will reduce the volume and frequency of specific Jordan retro launches. If this sounds familiar, that’s because it is: Nike faced a similar problem with Jordan nearly a decade ago, after ramping up production left too many sneakers sitting on shelves. Its solution then was the same as it is now: make fewer shoes and create a “pull market” where consumers chase rare shoes. “When consumers see the Jumpman, it should feel special,” Hill said. “It should feel earned. And every decision we're making is designed to ensure the Jordan Brand remains as coveted a decade from now as it has been for the past several decades” The revamp comes as the company reported quarterly financials that disappointed investors. On Thursday, Nike reported: Quarterly earnings per share at $0.48, more than the $0.43 analysts were expecting. But also reported $11.2 billion in sales for the quarter, less than the 11.3 billion expected, and about a 4% decline year over year. Nike said it expects sales to decline by “high-single digits” in the fiscal year. The company’s biggest sales decline is in China, where revenue plunged 26% year over year. The company’s gloomy guidance “assumes that China actually gets worse from a revenue perspective for the balance of this year,” CFO Dave Denton told analysts. “Correcting these issues will take time and an inflection back to sales growth is now not likely until calendar 2028, at the earliest,” analysts at Telsey Group wrote in a Friday note. Over the past few years, Nike has battled with a medley of issues: tariffs on imported goods, a “cautious” consumer, and increasing competition from footwear upstarts like Hoka and On, as well as old competitors like New Balance and Adidas .
